claim: Triple-drug therapies have transformed HIV from a fatal condition to a chronic one.
source: Triple-drug therapies have transformed HIV from a fatal condition to a chronic one.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in HIV treatment history, supported by clinical outcomes and epidemiological data.

claim: Triple-drug therapies should prevent HIV drug resistance evolution because one or more drugs suppress any partially resistant viruses.
source: These therapies should prevent HIV drug resistance evolution, because one or more drugs suppress any partially resistant viruses.
evidence: This represents the theoretical basis for triple-drug therapy design.

claim: Triple-drug therapies drastically reduced, but did not eliminate, resistance evolution.
source: In practice, such therapies drastically reduced, but did not eliminate, resistance evolution.
evidence: This is supported by clinical trial data and cohort studies showing ongoing resistance despite triple-drug therapy.

claim: HIV resistance evolves even after years on successful therapy.
source: resistance evolves (1) even after years on successful therapy
evidence: This is demonstrated through reanalysis of published cohort data showing ongoing resistance evolution.

claim: HIV resistance evolves sequentially, often via one mutation at a time.
source: resistance evolves (1) even after years on successful therapy, (2) sequentially, often via one mutation at a time
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of viral sequences showing partially resistant genotypes.

claim: HIV resistance evolves in a partially predictable order.
source: resistance evolves (1) even after years on successful therapy, (2) sequentially, often via one mutation at a time and (3) in a partially predictable order.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of clinical trial data showing consistent patterns of which drugs fail first.

claim: Better anti-retroviral therapies have drastically improved the lifespan of individuals living with HIV.
source: Better anti-retroviral therapies have drastically improved the lifespan of individuals living with HIV (Marcus et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marcus et al., 2020.

claim: Better anti-retroviral therapies prevent the evolution of drug resistance.
source: Better anti-retroviral therapies have drastically improved the lifespan of individuals living with HIV (Marcus et al., 2020) by preventing the evolution of drug resistance (Zazzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zazzi et al., 2018.

claim: When the first HIV drugs were introduced, drug resistance evolved in nearly all treated individuals in the first 6 months of treatment.
source: When the first HIV drugs were introduced, drug resistance evolved in nearly all treated individuals in the first 6 months of treatment (Larder et al., 1989)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Larder et al., 1989.

claim: Drug resistance sometimes evolved within weeks when the first HIV drugs were introduced.
source: drug resistance evolved in nearly all treated individuals in the first 6 months of treatment (Larder et al., 1989), and sometimes within weeks (Schuurman et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schuurman et al., 1995.

claim: Early HIV drug resistance was often encoded by single mutations conferring strong resistance.
source: This drug resistance, often encoded by single mutations conferring strong resistance (Larder and Kemp, 1989; Günthard et al., 2019), led to rebounding viral populations and treatment failure.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Larder and Kemp, 1989 and Günthard et al., 2019.

claim: Early HIV drug resistance led to rebounding viral populations and treatment failure.
source: This drug resistance, often encoded by single mutations conferring strong resistance (Larder and Kemp, 1989; Günthard et al., 2019), led to rebounding viral populations and treatment failure.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established clinical outcomes.

claim: Triple-drug therapies were introduced in 1995.
source: Triple-drug therapies, introduced in 1995, were expected to prevent the evolution of drug resistance and subsequent treatment failure (Hammer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a historical fact about HIV treatment.

claim: Triple-drug therapies were expected to prevent the evolution of drug resistance and subsequent treatment failure.
source: Triple-drug therapies, introduced in 1995, were expected to prevent the evolution of drug resistance and subsequent treatment failure (Hammer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hammer et al., 1997.

claim: Each of three drugs individually brings the expected number of viruses produced by a single infected cell (R0) below one, causing the viral population to shrink.
source: each of three drugs individually brings the expected number of viruses produced by a single infected cell (the basic reproductive number, R0) below one, causing the viral population to shrink.
evidence: This represents the theoretical mechanism of how triple-drug therapy should work.

claim: Mutations do not confer resistance across multiple classes of anti-retrovirals.
source: Because mutations do not confer resistance across multiple classes of anti-retrovirals (unlike many cases of bacterial resistance)
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV drug resistance mechanisms.

claim: If a virus gets a mutation conferring resistance to one drug, the two other drugs keep the R0 of that virus below one.
source: even if a virus gets a mutation conferring resistance to one drug, the two other drugs keep the R0 of that virus below one, and so viruses carrying this mutation cannot increase in number (Nowak and May, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nowak and May, 2000 and represents theoretical modeling.

claim: The probability of multiple mutations emerging simultaneously in a single round of replication is exceedingly small.
source: Despite HIV's high mutation rate, the probability of multiple mutations emerging simultaneously in a single round of replication is exceedingly small (Perelson and Nelson, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Perelson and Nelson, 1999.

claim: Triple-drug combination therapies saved many lives.
source: However, while triple-drug combination therapies saved many lives (Hogg et al., 1999; Walensky et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hogg et al., 1999 and Walensky et al., 2006.

claim: HIV has continued to evolve drug resistance into the modern day.
source: HIV has continued to evolve drug resistance into the modern day (Lee et al., 2014; Rocheleau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014 and Rocheleau et al., 2018.

claim: In the M98-863 clinical trial, 327 participants were randomized to receive treatment with 3TC, D4T, and NFV.
source: In a clinical trial (M98-863) conducted internationally, 327 participants were randomized to receive treatment with two NRTIs, 3TC (lamivudine) and D4T (stavudine), and a protease inhibitor, NFV (nelfinavir) (Kempf et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kempf et al., 2004.

claim: Within the first 2 years of therapy in the Kempf study, drug resistance was detected in 79 of the 327 patients (24%).
source: Within the first 2 years of therapy, drug resistance was detected in 79 of the 327 patients (24%).
evidence: This is data from the Kempf et al., 2004 study.

claim: In the Kempf study, roughly half of resistance cases occurred in the first year of treatment and half in the second year.
source: Kaplan-Meier plots in the original paper show that roughly half of these cases occurred in the first year of treatment and half in the second year
evidence: This is data from Kaplan-Meier plots in the Kempf et al., 2004 study.

claim: In the Kempf study, out of 79 individuals with resistance, approximately half carried resistance to one drug, half carried resistance to two drugs, and eight patients had resistance to three drugs.
source: Out of these 79 individuals with resistance, approximately half carried resistance to one drug, half carried resistance to two drugs, and eight patients had resistance to three drugs.
evidence: This is data from the Kempf et al., 2004 study.

claim: In the Kempf study, all 35 patients with resistance to one drug had resistance to 3TC.
source: All 35 patients with resistance to one drug had resistance to 3TC
evidence: This is data from the Kempf et al., 2004 study.

claim: In the Kempf study, 35 of 36 patients with resistance to two drugs had resistance to 3TC and NFV.
source: 35 of 36 patients with resistance to two drugs had resistance to 3TC and the PI (NFV).
evidence: This is data from the Kempf et al., 2004 study.

claim: On 3TC+D4T+NFV treatment, drugs fail in a consistent order: 3TC resistance arises first, then NFV resistance, and finally D4T resistance.
source: these data strongly suggest that on 3TC+D4T+NFV treatment, drugs fail in a consistent order: 3TC resistance arises first, then NFV resistance, and finally D4T resistance
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-sectional data in the Kempf et al., 2004 study.

claim: In the Hoffmann study, 48 of 68 genotyped patients who experienced virologic failure had drug resistance mutations.
source: Most of the patients experiencing virologic failure who were genotyped (48/68) had drug resistance mutations.
evidence: This is data from Hoffmann et al., 2009.

claim: In the Hoffmann study, of genotyped patients with resistance, 21 had resistance to just one drug, 20 had resistance to two drugs, and 3 had resistance to all three drugs.
source: Of these genotyped patients, 21 had resistance to just one drug, 20 had resistance to two drugs, and 3 had resistance to all three drugs.
evidence: This is data from Hoffmann et al., 2009.

claim: In the Hoffmann study, 19 of the singly resistant populations were resistant to EFV and just two had resistance to 3TC.
source: 19 of the singly resistant populations were resistant to EFV (the NNRTI) and just two had resistance to 3TC.
evidence: This is data from Hoffmann et al., 2009.

claim: In the Hoffmann study, all patients resistant to two drugs had resistance to EFV and 3TC.
source: All patients resistant to two drugs had resistance to EFV and 3TC.
evidence: This is data from Hoffmann et al., 2009.

claim: On 3TC+AZT+EFV treatment, EFV fails first and 3TC fails second.
source: These data strongly suggest that on 3TC+AZT+EFV treatment, drugs again fail in a consistent order, although a different order from the PI-based treatment. Here, EFV failed first (Figure 1B), and 3TC only second
evidence: This is inferred from data in Hoffmann et al., 2009 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 3TC resistance can evolve extremely quickly when 3TC is used as a monotherapy.
source: It is well-known that 3TC resistance can evolve extremely quickly when 3TC is used as a monotherapy (Feder et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feder et al., 2021a.

claim: 3TC resistance evolves first when it is co-administered with AZT.
source: 3TC resistance also evolves first when it is co-administered with AZT (Picard et al., 2001; Larder et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Picard et al., 2001 and Larder et al., 1995.

claim: 3TC resistance evolves first when co-administered with D4T and NFV.
source: and as we showed in the previous paragraph, it evolves first when co-administered with D4T and the PI NFV.
evidence: This is based on data presented earlier in the manuscript from the Kempf study.

claim: When 3TC is co-administered with an NNRTI, it appears to not be selected unless NNRTI resistance has already appeared.
source: It is therefore somewhat unexpected that when co-administered with an NNRTI, it appears to not be selected unless NNRTI resistance has already appeared.
evidence: This is based on data from the Hoffmann study presented earlier.

claim: Resistance evolution remained common even in individuals who started on a triple-drug regimen in the mid-1990s or later.
source: Resistance emerged not only in individuals who had started their treatment before 1995 on mono- or double-drug therapies, but also in individuals who started on a triple-drug regimen in the mid-1990s or later.
evidence: This is based on cohort studies.

claim: Several studies found substantial ongoing resistance evolution on both NNRTI-based and PI-based treatments even 5 or more years after starting therapy.
source: Several studies (Rocheleau et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2005) following cohorts of HIV-infected individuals over time found substantial ongoing resistance evolution on both NNRTI-based and PI-based treatments even 5 or more years after starting therapy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rocheleau et al., 2018 and Phillips et al., 2005.

claim: Cases of resistance accumulate over time in cohorts, suggesting that the yearly probability of resistance evolution does not rapidly decline to 0.
source: In these cohorts, cases of resistance accumulate over time, suggesting that the yearly probability of resistance evolution does not rapidly decline to 0.
evidence: This is inferred from cohort study data.

claim: Across all four drug categories (NNRTIs, PIs, non-3TC/FTC NRTIs and 3TC/FTC), the yearly conditional probability of resistance stays elevated above 0 even 5 or more years after the start of therapy.
source: We observe across all four drug categories (NNRTIs, PIs, non-3TC/FTC NRTIs and 3TC/FTC), the yearly conditional probability of resistance stays elevated above 0 even 5 or more years after the start of therapy (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on conditional survival analysis of the British Columbia cohort data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The conditional survival probabilities are highest in the first year of therapy, and appear to decline thereafter.
source: The conditional survival probabilities are highest in the first year of therapy, and appear to decline thereafter.
evidence: This is observed from the conditional survival analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The relatively slow rates of decline suggest that the risk of drug resistance evolution on triple-drug therapy remains even in individuals who have been on successful treatment for years.
source: The relatively slow rates of decline (Supplementary file 3) suggest that the risk of drug resistance evolution on triple-drug therapy remains even in individuals who have been on successful treatment for years.
evidence: This is inferred from the exponential decay analysis of resistance probabilities.

claim: Resistance patterns are not driven by a subset of individuals who fail therapy quickly.
source: This highlights the importance of ongoing within-patient processes in treatment failure and suggests that resistance patterns are not driven by a subset of individuals who fail therapy quickly.
evidence: This is inferred from the ongoing resistance evolution observed over many years.

claim: Many sequences are detected with 0, 1, 2, or 3+ drug resistance mutations in individuals treated with three-drug combination therapies.
source: Across individuals treated with three-drug combination therapies based on two NRTIs paired with an NNRTI (top) or PI (bottom), many sequences are detected with 0, 1, 2, or 3+ drug resistance mutations in a large cohort (data source: Feder et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B using data from Feder et al., 2016a.

claim: Observing sequences with only one or two resistance mutations at virologic failure suggests that partial resistance can allow growth above the detectable viral load threshold.
source: Observing sequences with only one or two resistance mutations at this stage suggests that partial resistance can allow growth above the detectable viral load threshold.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of partially resistant genotypes at virologic failure.

claim: A singly-resistant virus should be suppressed by two other drugs and not expand and lead to virologic failure under the expected mechanism of triple-drug therapy.
source: This is surprising under how we believe triple-drug therapies should work, since a singly-resistant virus should be suppressed by two other drugs and not expand and lead to virologic failure.
evidence: This represents the theoretical expectation for triple-drug therapy.

claim: In individuals on PI-based therapies, the singly-resistant viral populations almost all carry a 3TC-resistance conferring mutation.
source: In individuals on PI-based therapies, the singly-resistant viral populations almost all carry a 3TC-resistance conferring mutation, suggesting that resistance to 3TC overwhelmingly occurs before resistance to either the other NRTI or the PI.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C using data from the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database.

claim: For all PI-based therapies, resistance to 3TC occurs more often than predicted by mutational target sizes or mutation rates.
source: We found that for all therapies, resistance to 3TC occurs more often than predicted (p < 0.05, one-sided binomial test with a Benjamini-Hochberg correction and 5% false discovery rate, Figure 2C, all test details given in Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing comparing observed frequencies to expected frequencies based on mutation rates.

claim: The M184V mutation incurs a substantial fitness cost.
source: the most common 3TC mutation, M184V, incurs a substantial fitness cost (Paredes et al., 2009; Jain et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paredes et al., 2009 and Jain et al., 2011.

claim: The fitness cost of M184V makes it unlikely to be present as standing genetic variation.
source: which should make it unlikely to be present as standing genetic variation (Simen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simen et al., 2009 and represents an inference about population genetics.

claim: In individuals treated with NNRTI-based therapies, single drug resistance mutations most often conferred resistance to NNRTIs.
source: In individuals treated with NNRTI-based therapies, single drug resistance mutations most often conferred resistance to NNRTIs (Figure 2C), suggesting NNRTI resistance occurred first.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C using data from the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database.

claim: In all NNRTI-based therapies except one, NNRTI resistance occurred more often than predicted by the relative mutation rates.
source: we found that in all therapies except one, NNRTI resistance occurred more often than predicted by the relative mutation rates (one-sided binomial test with 5% FDR and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing comparing observed to expected frequencies.

claim: Even when administered as monotherapy, HIV drugs cause sensitive viral populations to shrink.
source: Even when administered as monotherapy, drugs cause sensitive viral populations to shrink (Eron et al., 1995; Reiss et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eron et al., 1995 and Reiss et al., 1988.

claim: In a patient treated with AZT monotherapy, the treated viral population initially shrinks and only after 16 weeks does the viral population expand again to detectable levels.
source: As an example, we plot data from a patient treated with AZT monotherapy (Figure 3A). Initially, the treated viral population shrinks. Only after 16 weeks, the viral population expands again to detectable levels.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A, which is reprinted from Reiss et al., 1988.

claim: Hill dose-response curves have been measured in cell culture for anti-retroviral-treated HIV.
source: Measuring the ability of the drug-resistant and sensitive virus to replicate at different drug concentrations (i.e. the Hill dose-response curve, Figure 3B, Chou, 1976; Zhang et al., 2004; Sampah et al., 2011) helps explain the dynamics, and such curves have been measured in cell culture for anti-retroviral-treated HIV (Sampah et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chou, 1976; Zhang et al., 2004; and Sampah et al., 2011.

claim: At certain intermediate drug concentrations, the resistant mutant can grow (R0>1) and the sensitive strain cannot (R0<1).
source: At certain intermediate drug concentrations, the resistant mutant can grow (R0>1) and the sensitive strain cannot (R0<1) (Rosenbloom et al., 2012, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosenbloom et al., 2012 and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Drugs overpowering even resistant virus at high concentrations have been demonstrated empirically in experimental settings.
source: Drugs overpowering even resistant virus at high concentrations have been demonstrated empirically in experimental settings (Sampah et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sampah et al., 2011.

claim: Patient non-adherence and different rates of drug metabolism between individuals can lead to drug concentrations that drop below the required levels over time.
source: However, patient non-adherence and different rates of drug metabolism between individuals can lead to drug concentrations that drop below the required levels over time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pharmacokinetics and adherence.

claim: Variable drug concentrations over time have been widely recognized as a potential route to drug resistance.
source: This has been widely recognized as a potential route to drug resistance (Fox et al., 2008; Bangsberg et al., 2007; Harrigan et al., 2005; Chesney et al., 2000; Cadosch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Missed doses may result in drug depletion of quickly decaying drugs while slowly decaying drugs may remain in their mutant selection window.
source: Missed doses may result in drug depletion of quickly decaying drugs while slowly decaying drugs may remain in their mutant selection window.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacokinetic properties of drugs with different half-lives.

claim: Both NFV and D4T are expected to lose most of their suppression within 24 hr due to short half-lives and, in the case of D4T, low potency.
source: Both NFV and D4T are expected to lose most of their suppression within 24 hr due to short half-lives and, in the case of D4T, low potency (Rosenbloom et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosenbloom et al., 2012.

claim: If a patient misses a dose of 3TC+D4T+NFV, 3TC may quickly be the only potent drug present and enter its mutant selection window, allowing a 3TC-resistant genotype to spread.
source: If a patient misses a dose, 3TC may quickly be the only potent drug present and enter its mutant selection window, allowing a 3TC-resistant genotype to spread.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacokinetic properties of the three drugs.

claim: A temporal heterogeneity model of HIV drug resistance evolution can explain that resistance mutations often emerge one mutation at a time and can lead to clinically detectable viral loads.
source: Consistent with clinical observations, resistance mutations often emerge one mutation at a time and can lead to clinically detectable viral loads (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on simulations of the temporal heterogeneity model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A temporal heterogeneity model produces instances of virologic failure without any resistance mutations, presumably in individuals with particularly poor adherence.
source: This model also produced instances of virologic failure without any resistance mutations, presumably in individuals with particularly poor adherence.
evidence: This is based on simulations of the temporal heterogeneity model.

claim: In the temporal heterogeneity model, when resistance did evolve, mutations occur in a predictable order and resistance to 3TC always precedes NFV and D4T.
source: Also in agreement with clinical observations, when resistance did evolve, mutations occur in a predictable order and resistance to 3TC always precedes NFV and D4T.
evidence: This is based on simulations of the temporal heterogeneity model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the temporal heterogeneity model, resistance overwhelmingly emerges in the first year of treatment when the population size is large, but then falls to quite low levels for the next years.
source: In disagreement with clinical observations, we find that resistance overwhelmingly emerges in the first year of treatment when the population size is large, but then falls to quite low levels for the next years.
evidence: This is based on simulations of the temporal heterogeneity model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 95.3% of the simulated individuals in the temporal heterogeneity model who did not develop resistance in the first year had suppressed HIV populations for the entire simulated 10-year treatment period.
source: 95.3% of the simulated individuals who did not develop resistance in the first year had suppressed HIV populations for the entire simulated 10-year treatment period.
evidence: This is based on simulations of the temporal heterogeneity model.

claim: Under a simple model of non-adherence for 3TC+D4T+NFV, potentially little resistance evolves after initial viral suppression.
source: This suggests that under a simple model of non-adherence for 3TC+D4T+NFV, potentially little resistance evolves after initial viral suppression
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results of the temporal heterogeneity model.

claim: NNRTIs have particularly long half-lives.
source: Unlike PIs, NNRTIs have particularly long half-lives (Taylor et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2007.

claim: Treatment interruptions of a few days are long enough for non-NNRTIs to leave the system, but short enough for NNRTIs to remain present.
source: Treatment interruptions of a few days are long enough for non-NNRTIs to leave the system, but short enough for NNRTIs to remain present.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacokinetic properties of NNRTIs versus other drug classes.

claim: In the SMART trial, 'covering' the NNRTI tail with additional shorter lived drugs did not affect the risk of drug resistance evolution.
source: It turned out that 'covering' the tail did not affect the risk of drug resistance evolution (Fox et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fox et al., 2008.

claim: The tail of NNRTI monotherapy may not be the reason NNRTI drug resistance evolves.
source: suggesting that the tail of NNRTI monotherapy may not be the reason NNRTI drug resistance evolves.
evidence: This is inferred from the results of the SMART trial.

claim: An increase in population size during a treatment interruption allows resistance mutations to accumulate as standing genetic variation, and when treatment resumes, these mutations increase in frequency due to selection.
source: We (Pennings) have proposed another explanation, namely that an increase in population size during an interruption allows resistance mutations to accumulate as standing genetic variation. When treatment resumes, these mutations increase in frequency due to selection (Pennings, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pennings, 2012.

claim: HIV drugs do not penetrate throughout the body uniformly and penetration profiles differ among drugs.
source: HIV drugs do not penetrate throughout the body uniformly and penetration profiles differ among drugs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV drug pharmacology.

claim: Even in triple-drug-treated individuals, parts of the body (e.g. brain, lymph nodes) may experience monotherapy.
source: As a result, even in triple-drug-treated individuals, parts of the body (e.g. brain, lymph nodes) may experience monotherapy (Else et al., 2011; Letendre et al., 2008; Decloedt et al., 2015; Fletcher et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: 3TC, NFV, and D4T have differential rates of penetrance into the brain, with penetrances of NFV and D4T particularly poor.
source: 3TC, NFV, and D4T have differential rates of penetrance into the brain, with penetrances of NFV and D4T particularly poor (Letendre et al., 2008; Browne et al., 1993; Aweeka et al., 1999; Ene et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Differential drug penetrance can create parts of the brain where 3TC-resistant HIV can effectively replicate and spread, potentially allowing detection in the blood as a 3TC-resistant type.
source: This can create parts of the brain where 3TC-resistant HIV can effectively replicate and spread, potentially allowing detection in the blood as a 3TC-resistant type.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential penetrance profiles of the drugs.

claim: A spatial heterogeneity model of HIV drug resistance evolution produced all three features observed in clinical data (ongoing, sequential, and predictable resistance evolution), but only for 3TC.
source: We found that this model of spatial heterogeneity produced all three features that we observed in the clinical data under three-drug combination therapies, but only for one of the drugs in the combination - 3TC (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on simulations of the spatial heterogeneity model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the spatial heterogeneity model, 3TC resistance continues to emerge, even if individuals have been on therapy for several years.
source: First, 3TC resistance continues to emerge, even if individuals have been on therapy for several years.
evidence: This is based on simulations of the spatial heterogeneity model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the spatial heterogeneity model, individuals with larger population sizes evolve resistance more rapidly than those with smaller population sizes.
source: Individuals with larger population sizes evolve resistance more rapidly than those with smaller population sizes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 from the spatial heterogeneity model simulations.

claim: In the spatial heterogeneity model, resistance mutations exclusively emerge one at a time and can lead to clinically detectable levels.
source: Second, resistance mutations exclusively emerge one at a time and can lead to clinically detectable levels.
evidence: This is based on simulations of the spatial heterogeneity model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the spatial heterogeneity model, resistance mutations occur in a predictable order, with overwhelmingly resistance to 3TC and no ongoing resistance to NFV and D4T.
source: Third, resistance mutations occur in a predictable order, and we see overwhelmingly resistance to 3TC and no ongoing resistance to NFV and D4T.
evidence: This is based on simulations of the spatial heterogeneity model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Compartments with additional patterns of drug penetrance are necessary to provoke additional resistance evolution beyond 3TC in the spatial heterogeneity model.
source: This suggests that compartments with additional patterns of drug penetrance are necessary to provoke additional resistance evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations of the current spatial heterogeneity model.

claim: NNRTIs tend to have strong penetration profiles, which may explain why drug resistance to NNRTIs emerges first.
source: NNRTIs tend to have strong penetration profiles, which may explain why drug resistance to NNRTIs emerges first (Figures 1B and 2C).
evidence: This is speculated based on known NNRTI pharmacology and observed resistance patterns.

claim: Many NNRTIs are highly suppressive even at relatively low concentrations and sometimes even for genotypes with resistance mutations.
source: However, many NNRTIs are highly suppressive even at relatively low concentrations and sometimes even for genotypes with resistance mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NNRTI pharmacology.

claim: NNRTI resistance evolution may require not only a single drug compartment but also a sub-clinical concentration of the NNRTI to select for resistance mutations.
source: This suggests that an NNRTI resistance evolution may require not only a single drug compartment (i.e. the absence of other drugs), but also a sub-clinical concentration of the NNRTI to select for resistance mutations.
evidence: This is speculated based on the properties of NNRTIs.

claim: In a model of spatial or temporal heterogeneity, a desirable property (high penetration or long half-life) actually makes a drug vulnerable to resistance.
source: However, in a model of spatial or temporal heterogeneity, a desirable property –high penetration or long half-life– actually makes a drug vulnerable to resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanisms of the spatial and temporal heterogeneity models.

claim: The best way to prevent the evolution of 3TC resistance (when treatment is with 3TC+NFV+D4T) is not to target the shortcomings of 3TC, but to target the shortcomings of the other drugs.
source: Therefore, the best way to prevent the evolution of 3TC resistance (when treatment is with 3TC+NFV+D4T) is not to target the shortcomings of 3TC, but to target the shortcomings of the other drugs.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanisms of spatial and temporal heterogeneity models.

claim: If 3TC monotherapy occurs in space or time because of a long half-life or good penetration, the solution would be to add another drug that also has a long half-life or good penetration.
source: Specifically, if 3TC monotherapy occurs in space or time because of a long half-life or good penetration, the solution would be to add another drug that also has a long half-life or good penetration.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanisms of spatial and temporal heterogeneity models.

claim: Ritonavir-'boosted' lopinavir (LPV/r) resulted in improved penetance and extended half-life in comparison to NFV.
source: In particular, ritonavir-'boosted' lopinavir (LPV/r) (Tseng et al., 2015) resulted in improved penetance and extended half-life in comparison to NFV (Capparelli et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tseng et al., 2015 and Capparelli et al., 2005.

claim: Replacing NFV with LPV/r in the Kempf study resulted in a substantial reduction of resistance evolution by 76%.
source: The clinical effect of replacing NFV with LPV/r in the previously described Kempf study (Kempf et al., 2004) is a substantial reduction of resistance evolution by 76%.
evidence: This is based on data from the Kempf et al., 2004 study.

claim: In the NFV arm of the Kempf study, 79 of 327 individuals developed some type of drug resistance (24%) within 2 years, whereas in the LPV/r arm, only 19 of 326 did (6%).
source: In the NFV arm of the study, 79 of 327 individuals developed some type of drug resistance (24%) within 2 years, whereas in the LPV/r arm, only 19 of 326 did (6%).
evidence: This is data from the Kempf et al., 2004 study.

claim: LPV/r consistently reaches a level above the 50% inhibitory concentration in cerebrospinal fluid.
source: In the context of resistance evolution via spatially-varying drugs, LPV/r consistently reaches a level above the 50% inhibitory concentration in cerebrospinal fluid (Capparelli et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Capparelli et al., 2005.

claim: The enhanced spatial coverage of LPV/r likely shrinks the size or number of compartments in which 3TC exists alone.
source: thereby likely shrinking the size or number of compartments in which 3TC exists alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the improved penetrance of LPV/r.

claim: The fourfold lower rate of drug resistance evolution among individuals on the LPV/r regimen suggests that the enhanced spatial coverage of LPV/r decreased the portions of the body where 3TC reached alone by a factor of four.
source: The fourfold lower rate of drug resistance evolution among individuals on the LPV/r regimen suggests that the enhanced spatial coverage of LPV/r decreased the portions of the body where 3TC reached alone by a factor of four.
evidence: This is inferred from the clinical data comparing NFV and LPV/r.

claim: A model of spatial heterogeneity can recreate the observed clinical patterns (ongoing, sequential and predictable evolution) for resistance to specific drugs but not others.
source: We extended existing one or two drug models for imperfect adherence and imperfect drug penetrance and found that a model of spatial heterogeneity can recreate the observed clinical patterns – ongoing, sequential and predictable evolution – for resistance to specific drugs but not others.
evidence: This is based on the simulation results presented in Figure 5B.

claim: A temporal model readily matches certain observations (sequential and predictably ordered mutations), but not others (namely, ongoing resistance after years on therapy).
source: A temporal model readily matches certain observations (sequential and predictably ordered mutations), but not others (namely, ongoing resistance after years on therapy).
evidence: This is based on the simulation results presented in Figure 5A.

claim: We have two possible explanations for the observation that drug resistance can evolve during triple-drug therapies, neither of which currently explain all aspects of the data in their current state.
source: Therefore, we have two possible explanations for the observation that drug resistance can evolve during triple-drug therapies, neither of which currently explain all aspects of the data in their current state.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results.

claim: While we know that temporal and spatial heterogeneity exist and can cause drug resistance evolution, this does not prove that they do.
source: Further, while we know that temporal and spatial heterogeneity exist and can cause drug resistance evolution, this does not prove that they do.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the limitations of the models.

claim: There is some evidence that the NNRTI tail does not explain NNRTI drug resistance in low-adherence patients.
source: Yet, there is some evidence that the NNRTI tail does not explain NNRTI drug resistance in low-adherence patients (see discussion under temporal heterogeneity).
evidence: This refers to evidence discussed earlier about the SMART trial.

claim: In the temporal heterogeneity model of incomplete adherence, many individuals stayed virologically suppressed despite poor adherence.
source: In our model of temporal heterogeneity in drug levels through incomplete adherence (of PIs, not NNRTIs), many individuals stayed virologically suppressed despite poor adherence.
evidence: This is based on simulation results from the temporal heterogeneity model.

claim: Even though drug conditions intermittently select for drug resistant variants in the temporal heterogeneity model, viral populations could not reach critical population sizes rapidly enough to produce the relevant variants that could spread.
source: Even though drug conditions intermittently select for drug resistant variants, viral populations could not reach critical population sizes rapidly enough to produce the relevant variants that could spread.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results of the temporal heterogeneity model.

claim: A quantitative approach that includes mutant selection windows, pharmacokinetics and population genetics is needed to adjudicate between potential explanations for a variety of drug combinations.
source: While outside the scope of this study, we propose that a quantitative approach that includes mutant selection windows, pharmacokinetics and population genetics is needed to adjudicate between potential explanations for a variety of drug combinations.
evidence: This is a proposal for future research directions.

claim: Detailed models of HIV drug resistance have already been developed, especially for models of temporal heterogeneity.
source: Detailed models of HIV drug resistance have already been developed, especially for models of temporal heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a statement about the existing literature.

claim: Rosenbloom et al., 2012 examined how adherence patterns for a two-drug therapy (boosted darunivir and raltegravir, DRV/r + RAL) affected the mode and rate of resistance evolution.
source: For example, in a carefully parameterized HIV model focused largely on single drugs (Rosenbloom et al., 2012), the authors examined how adherence patterns for a two-drug therapy (boosted darunivir and raltegravir, DRV/r + RAL) affected the mode and rate of resistance evolution.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosenbloom et al., 2012.

claim: Rosenbloom et al., 2012 found that virologic failure could occur from a viral population resistant to raltegravir but not darunivir, because of the characteristics of the darunivir mutant selection window.
source: They found that virologic failure could occur from a viral population resistant to raltegravir but not darunivir, because of the characteristics of the darunivir mutant selection window.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosenbloom et al., 2012.

claim: Bershteyn and Eckhoff, 2013 examined drug resistance dynamics in individuals taking PrEP (TDF) under a realistic model of non-adherence.
source: Similarly, Bershteyn and Eckhoff, 2013 examined drug resistance dynamics in individuals taking PrEP (TDF) under a realistic model of non-adherence.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bershteyn and Eckhoff, 2013.

claim: No three-drug therapies were examined in previous detailed models of temporal heterogeneity.
source: However, these analyses of one or two drug combinations served as proofs of concept, and no three-drug therapies were examined.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing models.

claim: It is not possible to make quantitative comparisons between models and patient data and test how spatial and temporal variation of drug levels contributes to HIV multi-drug resistance evolution on triple-drug therapies.
source: A real gap therefore remains in developing realistic models that can explain complex patterns of resistance emergence under the most widely used triple-drug therapies.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: The gap between the models and clinical data is even larger for spatial models than for temporal models, because the models that have been studied are simpler.
source: For the spatial models, the gap between the models and clinical data is even larger than for the temporal models, because the models that have been studied are simpler (Perelson et al., 1997; Moreno-Gamez et al., 2015; Lorenzo-Redondo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing spatial models.

claim: Many parameters for spatial models remain unknown.
source: Filling this gap will be particularly challenging because many parameters remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in developing spatial models.

claim: Understanding where, when, and how certain drugs reach different parts of the body is complicated.
source: Understanding where, when, and how certain drugs reach different parts of the body is complicated (Vendel et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vendel et al., 2019.

claim: Different studies have found different relative penetrances of drugs into the tissue versus the plasma.
source: and indeed, different studies have found different relative penetrances of drugs into the tissue versus the plasma.
evidence: This is a statement about inconsistencies in the literature.

claim: The administered version of a drug may be at a different concentration than the active form.
source: First, the administered version of a drug may be at a different concentration than the active form (Dumond et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dumond et al., 2008.

claim: The intracellular concentration of a drug, rather than the tissue concentration, may mediate effectiveness.
source: Second, the intracellular concentration of a drug, rather than the tissue concentration, may mediate effectiveness, requiring that we understand not only whether drugs reach a tissue, but the rates at which they are transported into cells (Bazzoli et al., 2010; Dumond et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bazzoli et al., 2010 and Dumond et al., 2008.

claim: There can be considerable heterogeneity of drug penetrance even within a single lymph node or gut cross-section.
source: For example, there can be considerable heterogeneity of drug penetrance even within a single lymph node or gut cross-section (Thompson et al., 2015; Thompson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thompson et al., 2015 and Thompson et al., 2019.

claim: Many studies report tissue drug concentrations relative to the blood plasma, without considering the actual tissue drug level and its inhibitory effect on the virus.
source: Fourth, many studies report tissue drug concentrations relative to the blood plasma, without considering the actual tissue drug level and its inhibitory effect on the virus (Else et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Else et al., 2011.

claim: Comparing tissue drug concentration to the IC50 does not capture the full dynamics of drug concentrations within the body.
source: Even comparing tissue drug concentration to the IC50 does not capture the full dynamics of drug concentrations within the body (Shen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2008.

claim: Treatment with other drugs (e.g. tuberculosis drugs) may affect the half-lives and penetration of HIV drugs.
source: For example, treatment with other drugs (e.g. tuberculosis drugs) may affect the half-lives and penetration of HIV drugs (López-Cortés et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to López-Cortés et al., 2002.

claim: Genetic variation among treated individuals may mediate drug penetrance.
source: Genetic variation among treated individuals may also mediate penetrance (see Apostolova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Apostolova et al., 2015.

claim: Efavirenz concentrations are higher in people with certain genotypes, and these genotypes are more common in Black/African groups.
source: For example, efavirenz concentrations are higher in people with certain genotypes, and these genotypes are more common in Black/African groups.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pharmacogenetics of efavirenz.

claim: Rates of drug metabolism differ between men and women.
source: Rates of drug metabolism also differ between men and women (Else et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Else et al., 2011.

claim: Different adherence patterns could hypothetically make different mutational orderings more or less likely.
source: Different adherence patterns could hypothetically make different mutational orderings more or less likely as well.
evidence: This is speculation about how adherence might affect resistance patterns.

claim: The combination of imperfect adherence with imperfect penetration makes sequential drug resistance evolution likely in an in vitro system.
source: A recent paper suggests that the combination of imperfect adherence with imperfect penetration makes sequential drug resistance evolution likely in an in vitro system (Lustig et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lustig et al., 2019.

claim: It remains unclear if temporal heterogeneity, spatial heterogeneity, or a combination of the two cause the evolution of drug resistance during triple-drug therapy.
source: For now, it remains unclear if temporal heterogeneity, spatial heterogeneity, or a combination of the two cause the evolution of drug resistance during triple-drug therapy.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Clarity on whether temporal or spatial heterogeneity causes resistance will aid the rational design of treatments that minimize the risk of resistance evolution.
source: Clarity on this important unresolved mystery will aid the rational design of treatments that minimize the risk of resistance evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical implications of understanding resistance mechanisms.

claim: Mathematical modeling has played an essential role throughout the HIV pandemic.
source: Mathematical modeling has played an essential role throughout the HIV pandemic
evidence: This is a statement about the history of HIV research.

claim: Early HIV modeling studies helped motivate the need for triple-drug therapies.
source: Indeed, these studies helped motivate the need for triple-drug therapies in the first place (Perelson and Nelson, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Perelson and Nelson, 1999.

claim: Future studies addressing the evolution of multi-drug resistance in HIV should use realistic parameters and grapple with the pharmacokinetics of multiple drugs and how they interact.
source: Future studies addressing the evolution of multi-drug resistance in HIV should use realistic parameters (for example, like Rosenbloom et al., 2012 and Bershteyn and Eckhoff, 2013) and will need to grapple with the pharmacokinetics of multiple drugs and how they interact (Koizumi and Iwami, 2014; Jilek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Experimental work has highlighted drug pairs that suppress in vitro viral populations to both greater and lesser extents than each drug working independently.
source: Experimental work has highlighted drug pairs that suppress in vitro viral populations to both greater and lesser extents than each drug working independently, which may provide a partial answer to why some combinations of drugs fail at a surprisingly high rate (Jilek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jilek et al., 2012.

claim: Future studies should not just match viral loads and rates of patient failure, but also genetic patterns of resistance.
source: These future studies should not just match viral loads and rates of patient failure, but also genetic patterns of resistance.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Drug resistance rates have fallen over time.
source: drug resistance rates have fallen over time (Feder et al., 2016a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feder et al., 2016a.

claim: Virologic failure varies as a function of adherence.
source: virologic failure varies as a function of adherence (Harrigan et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harrigan et al., 2005.

claim: Virologic failure varies between different drug combinations.
source: virologic failure varies as a function of adherence (Harrigan et al., 2005) and between different drug combinations (Lee et al., 2014; Feder et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014 and Feder et al., 2016a.

claim: Expanded models will allow predictions about rates and patterns of resistance for novel combinations of drugs.
source: We hope that expanded models will allow us not only to make predictions – for example, about rates and patterns of resistance for novel combinations of drugs
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of future models.

claim: Patterns of resistance can be used to estimate how large single-drug compartments are, or how rapidly viruses migrate between different parts of the body.
source: For example, can we use patterns of resistance to estimate how large single-drug compartments are, or how rapidly viruses migrate between different parts of the body (Feder et al., 2019)?
evidence: This is a question about potential applications of models, with a citation to Feder et al., 2019.

claim: Drug resistance represents a serious threat across disease systems.
source: Drug resistance represents a serious threat across disease systems
evidence: This is established knowledge about drug resistance.

claim: Spatial and temporal variation in drug levels likely contribute to drug resistance in other disease systems.
source: and spatial and temporal variation in drug levels likely contribute in these other instances as well.
evidence: This is speculation about the generalizability of HIV resistance mechanisms.

claim: Many in the cancer community argue that applying multiple drugs simultaneously should halt the evolution of resistance.
source: For example, while many in the cancer community argue that applying multiple drugs simultaneously should halt the evolution of resistance (Basanta et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Basanta et al., 2012.

claim: Experimental evidence suggests multi-drug resistant cells may already exist as standing genetic variation in cancer.
source: experimental evidence also suggests multi-drug resistant cells may already exist as standing genetic variation (Bhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bhang et al., 2015.

claim: In treated solid tumors, drugs that cannot penetrate through the entire tumor may form a concentration gradient of selection pressure that may speed the evolution of resistance.
source: In treated solid tumors, drugs that cannot penetrate through the entire tumor may form a concentration gradient of selection pressure that theoretical (Hermsen et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2015; Gralka et al., 2017) and experimental (Baym et al., 2016) evidence suggests may speed the evolution of resistance.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: In tuberculosis, there is evidence that drug levels in various types of granulomas are often not as high as in the blood and do not reach bactericidal levels.
source: In tuberculosis, there is evidence that drug levels in various types of granulomas are often not as high as in the blood (and do not reach bactericidal levels) (Prideaux et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prideaux et al., 2015.

claim: Drug levels may be particularly low for some drugs in cavitary lesions in tuberculosis.
source: and may be particularly low for some drugs in cavitary lesions (Strydom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Strydom et al., 2019.

claim: Since not all tuberculosis patients have cavitary lesions, ideal drug choice or dosing may not be the same for all individuals.
source: Since not all tuberculosis patients have cavitary lesions, this means that ideal drug choice or dosing may not be the same for all individuals (Strydom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Strydom et al., 2019 and represents an inference about treatment implications.

claim: Lessons about spatial and temporal heterogeneity in drug concentrations in HIV can form a scaffold upon which we can try to understand resistance evolution in other disease systems.
source: Lessons about spatial and temporal heterogeneity in drug concentrations in HIV can form a scaffold upon which we can try to understand resistance evolution in other disease systems.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of HIV research.

claim: Every natural system experiences multiple stressors simultaneously.
source: Even apart from disease, every natural system experiences multiple stressors simultaneously
evidence: This is a general statement about evolutionary biology.

claim: How populations evolve in response to complex environments represents a fundamental question in evolutionary biology.
source: How populations evolve in response to complex environments represents a fundamental question in evolutionary biology.
evidence: This is a statement about fundamental questions in evolutionary biology.

claim: HIV represents a powerful study system for interrogating how populations evolve in response to complex environments.
source: In addition to (and perhaps because of) its medical relevance, HIV represents a powerful study system for interrogating this question.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of HIV as a model system.

claim: We understand many of HIV's population parameters relating to viral kinetics.
source: We understand many of its population parameters relating to viral kinetics
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge about HIV.

claim: Extensive research has produced a well-developed genotype-phenotype map of HIV resistance mutations.
source: and extensive research has produced a well-developed genotype-phenotype map of resistance mutations.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge about HIV resistance.

claim: Because drug resistance emerges repeatedly in different individuals, we can understand which features of intra-patient evolution are generalizable.
source: Because drug resistance emerges repeatedly in different individuals, we can understand which features of this intra-patient evolution are generalizable
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of studying HIV resistance.

claim: In theory, multi-drug therapies should suppress pathogen populations and prevent the evolution of resistance.
source: In theory, multi-drug therapies should suppress pathogen populations and prevent the evolution of resistance.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical basis for multi-drug therapies.

claim: In practice, multi-drug therapies are challenging to achieve, and pathogen populations do not experience all drugs in all places at all times.
source: In practice, multi-drug therapies are challenging to achieve, and pathogen populations do not experience all drugs in all places at all times.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges of multi-drug therapies.
